title: Numbers, text, and shapes
summary: Integers, floats, text, and the tuple and array shapes that group them.

blocks.html: Every value in Rust has a type, and the compiler checks types before the program ever runs. You rarely write the type out: given let n = 3; the compiler picks one for you. That is inference, and it is a convenience, not a promise that types do not matter.

blocks.title: integers come in sized boxes

blocks.html:
Integer types are a letter and a bit width. The letter says whether negative numbers are allowed: i for signed, u for unsigned. The number is how many bits of memory the value occupies.

  • i8 / u8 — 8 bits, so -128 to 127 or 0 to 255
  • i32 / u32 — 32 bits, the default choice for signed integers
  • i64 / u64 — 64 bits, for counts past the two billion an i32 can hold

Underscores in a number are decoration for the reader: 1_000_000 and 1000000 are the same value. Decimal numbers use f32 or f64, and an unannotated decimal is f64.

blocks.title: floats, booleans, characters, text
blocks.output:
2.5 false A in math
true, true

blocks.html: A char is one Unicode scalar value — one character, in single quotes. Double quotes make text: "math" is a string literal, and its type is &str. That & is the only unexplained symbol on this page; it earns its place in chapter 07. For now, single quotes hold one character and double quotes hold text.

Two shapes group values without any ceremony. A tuple packs a fixed number of values that may have different types, and you reach into it by position: .0, .1. A pattern like let (x, y) = point; unpacks the whole tuple at once; that is destructuring.

An array holds many values of one type, and its length is part of its type: [i32; 3] is three integers and never four. Ask it for .len(), read a slot with [index], and counting starts at zero.

blocks.title: arrays: length, indexing, the repeat form
casts and the integer division surprise

blocks.html:
Integer division throws the remainder away: 10 / 4 is 2, not 2.5. Convert with as before dividing and the decimals come back. as also changes width, and the bits that no longer fit are simply dropped: let big = 300; let small = big as u8; leaves small holding 44. A literal is checked instead — 300 as u8 does not compile at all.

Integer arithmetic is checked as well, in a debug build. Take an i8 holding 127, add 1, and the program stops with attempt to add with overflow rather than wrapping around. A release build wraps silently to -128, which is why the check exists while you develop.

quiz.q: The compiler has to pick a type for the 3 in let n = 3; on its own. Which type does it pick?
quiz.why: An integer with nothing else to go on is i32, the default signed 32-bit type. Later usage can force a different inference, but the fallback is i32.

quiz.q: Which type describes an array of exactly three i32 values?
quiz.why: An array type is written element type, semicolon, length. The parenthesized form is a tuple: same values, but grouping by field rather than by index.

quiz.q: What does 7 / 2 evaluate to when both values are integers?
quiz.why: Integer division truncates toward zero, so the fraction is discarded. Cast one side to f64 to get 3.5.

exercise.brief: Build a tuple holding the number 3 and the boolean true, and an array holding 10, 20, 30. Print the tuple's first field, the array's length, and the array's last element.
exercise.hint: Fields are read with pair.0 and slots with nums[0]. The last slot of a three-element array is nums[2], because counting starts at zero.
